nameStory: The "dove's-foot" part of this plant's name comes from the shape of its deeply divided leaves, which look remarkably like the delicate, spread toes of a dove's foot. The "crane's-bill" refers to the long, pointed seed pods that stretch out like a crane's beak after the flowers fade.
description: Dove's-foot crane's-bill is a small, low-growing annual wildflower that forms soft, sprawling mats close to the ground. This delicate plant rarely grows taller than 8-12 inches, with fuzzy, deeply-cut leaves that feel velvety to the touch. Its tiny pink or purple flowers appear in spring and early summer, followed by the characteristic long, pointed seed pods that give crane's-bills their name. The whole plant has a gentle, soft appearance and texture that makes it easy to overlook among other vegetation.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Deeply divided into 5-7 narrow segments that spread out like fingers or a bird's foot, with a distinctly soft, velvety texture that feels almost fuzzy when you gently rub it between your fingers

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small, delicate pink or light purple flowers about 1/4 inch across with 5 rounded petals and a subtle sweet fragrance, usually appearing in pairs

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, spreading annual that forms soft mats close to the ground, rarely standing more than a foot tall, with stems that feel tender and somewhat succulent

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Long, pointed seed pods that look like tiny crane beaks, splitting dramatically when ripe to launch seeds with a small popping sound you can sometimes hear

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Soft, hairy stems that are often reddish-tinged and feel slightly sticky or tacky when handled, branching from the base in a sprawling pattern

habitat: Look for dove's-foot crane's-bill in disturbed soils, garden edges, lawns, and waste areas throughout New England. It particularly thrives in sandy or gravelly soils and is often found along roadsides, in cultivated areas, and anywhere the ground has been recently disturbed. This adaptable little plant can tolerate both sun and partial shade.

seasonality.spring: Plants emerge early and begin blooming in late spring with their characteristic small pink flowers. The soft, dove's-foot shaped leaves are at their most distinctive during this season.
seasonality.summer: Flowering continues into early summer, followed by the development of the long, pointed seed pods that give crane's-bills their name. Plants may start to look worn in hot, dry weather.
seasonality.fall: Seeds have dispersed and annual plants are dying back, leaving little trace except possibly some dried stems in protected areas.
seasonality.winter: No above-ground parts remain visible, as this is an annual plant that completes its entire life cycle in one growing season.

funFact: When the seed pods ripen, they don't just open—they actually explode! The five sections of each "crane's beak" suddenly curl up and fling the seeds up to several feet away, sometimes making a tiny audible pop that you can hear if you're listening carefully on a quiet day.
confusionNotes: Dove's-foot crane's-bill is most easily confused with other small crane's-bills like small-flowered crane's-bill, but dove's-foot has much softer, more velvety leaves and the leaf divisions are more rounded at the tips rather than sharply pointed. Remember: dove's-foot feels like velvet, others feel more papery or rough.
contextualKnowledge: Don't confuse these wild geraniums with the common garden geraniums sold at nurseries—those are actually in the genus Pelargonium and are completely different plants! True geraniums like this one are also called "hardy geraniums" and are much more cold-tolerant than their showy garden cousins.
compareHints: Among New England's crane's-bills, dove's-foot stands out for its exceptionally soft, velvety leaf texture and low, mat-forming growth habit. While wild geranium has much larger, more deeply palmately-lobed leaves and taller growth, and Herb Robert has more finely cut, lacy leaves with a strong smell, dove's-foot crane's-bill keeps things simple with its gentle, fuzzy appearance and modest size.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Wild geranium stands out from its cranesbill cousins by its substantial size, soft pink flowers, and preference for rich woodlands.
Among New England's wild geraniums, Herb Robert is the most delicate and lacy-looking, with much more finely divided leaves than the larger Wild Geranium.
Among New England's crane's-bills, bloody crane's-bill stands out for its deeply divided leaves that are cut almost to the base, creating very narrow segments.
Among New England's crane's-bills, rock crane's-bill is unique for its low, mat-forming growth and intensely fragrant leaves - most others grow more upright and have much less scented foliage.
Northern cranesbill is much smaller and more delicate than wild geranium, with tiny lavender flowers instead of large pink ones.
Thunberg's Geranium is much smaller and more delicate than our common Wild Geranium, with more finely divided leaves and smaller flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Carolina crane's-bill has the smallest flowers - much tinier than the showy inch-wide blooms of wild geranium or the medium-sized flowers of Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, meadow crane's-bill is one of the largest and most robust, forming much bigger clumps than most relatives.

Among New England's crane's-bills, dusky crane's-bill is unique for its nearly black flowers with backward-curved petals - our native wild geranium has pink flowers that face upward, while Herb Robert has small bright pink flowers.
Among New England's crane's-bills, this is one of the tiniest and most easily overlooked.
Purple-vein geranium stands out from other New England geraniums primarily by its bright blue flowers - most other species have pink, white, or purple blooms.

Among New England's crane's-bills, cut-leaved crane's-bill stands out for having the most finely divided leaves - while wild geranium has broader, less deeply cut leaves and Herb Robert has more triangular leaf segments, cut-leaved crane's-bill looks almost feathery.
Among New England's crane's-bills, little-robin is the tiniest - much smaller than wild geranium or Herb Robert.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Long-stalked stands out for its exceptionally long flower stalks and deeply dissected leaves.

Richardson's geranium differs from New England's common wild geranium by having paler flowers with more prominent dark veining, perfectly straight (not curved) seed beaks, and more finely divided leaf segments.
Wood crane's-bill differs from our native wild geranium by having more deeply dissected leaves and typically stronger purple coloring with more prominent petal veining.
Among New England's crane's-bills, Siberian Crane's-bill would be one of the smallest and most delicate-looking species.
